messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Pharmacist
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Manaia was twenty-two when his younger brother, Tama, died. Tama had been at a party, a house gathering with friends from their old high school, and someone had brought a bottle of cheap whiskey. Manaia was at work that night, behind the pharmacy counter, when his phone lit up with a call from his mother. He still could not tell the story in any kind of order. There were fragments: his mother’s voice, high and strange; the drive to the hospital; the sight of Tama’s face, grey and still, on a gurney. The doctors said it was alcohol poisoning. They said Tama had been dared, or had dared himself, or had simply not known when to stop. Manaia had never been able to line the pieces up into something that made sense. When he tried to remember that night, his mind went blank, or else he felt a surge of guilt so sharp it made him nauseous—guilt that he had not been there, that he had not answered Tama’s last text, that he had been dispensing antibiotics for other people’s sore throats while his brother was dying. Sometimes, when he forced himself to think about the hospital room, he felt nothing at all. He could picture the fluorescent lights, the beeping machines, his mother’s hand in his, but it was like watching a scene from a movie about someone else’s life. That numbness scared him more than the guilt.

For two years now, Manaia had been living with a body that no longer trusted the world. He would be standing at the pharmacy counter, scanning a prescription bottle, and suddenly his heart would be pounding, his palms sweating, his breath coming in short gasps—and he would have no idea why. His body reacted before his mind could catch up. He had learned to brace himself constantly, his shoulders hunched, his jaw tight, waiting for something bad to happen. He often reacted as if he were in danger even when nothing was wrong. A customer raising their voice about a co-pay would send him into a full alarm state; a sudden loud noise from the back room would make him flinch so hard he dropped things. His pharmacist, a kind woman named Denise, had started to notice. She asked if he was sleeping. He lied and said yes.

The triggers were everywhere now, and they were strange. He could not stand the smell of alcohol. A patient would walk in reeking of beer from a lunch break, and Manaia’s throat would close. He would have to excuse himself to the bathroom, where he would grip the sink and breathe until the wave passed. He had stopped going to family gatherings because someone was always drinking. He had stopped seeing his old friends. He had stopped going anywhere, really, except to work and back to his apartment. Funerals were out of the question. When his great-aunt passed, he did not attend. He told his mother he could not get the time off. She had been quiet on the phone, and he knew she was hurt, but the thought of standing at a graveside made him feel like he was already dead himself.

The worst part, Manaia thought, was that he no longer recognized himself. He used to be happy. He used to laugh easily, to joke with customers, to call Tama after every shift and talk about nothing. Now he was miserable all the time, and he could not remember what it felt like to be any other way. His life felt destroyed. He went through the motions—filling prescriptions, checking inventory, going home, eating dinner, staring at the ceiling—but nothing felt meaningful anymore. He had become a pharmacist because he wanted to help people, because he wanted to be useful, but now every bottle he handed across the counter felt hollow. What was the point? He could not even save his own brother.

What finally brought Manaia to seek help was a Tuesday evening in early spring. He had been walking home from the pharmacy, and he passed a bar with its door open. The smell of whiskey spilled out onto the sidewalk. His body locked up, his vision tunneled, and he stood there frozen, breathing in the smell of the thing that had killed Tama, while people streamed past him on the street. He stood there for a long time. When he finally moved, he walked straight to his apartment, sat down on his couch, and called his mother. He told her he needed to talk to someone. He told her he did not want to feel like this anymore. She found him a therapist who specialized in trauma. He had his first appointment the following week. He was terrified—terrified that talking about it would make it worse, terrified that the therapist would tell him he was broken beyond repair, terrified that he would never feel like himself again. But he was also, for the first time in two years, hoping.
